No accounts, payments, GPS, public sharing or automatic personalisation. Expand beyond two quests only after the first test.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Collect opt-in email, random participant ID, chosen neighbourhood and optional completion/feedback; no GPS, home address or employer performance data. tests.fail: Any stale/unapproved/withdrawn delivery, duplicate or blind ambiguous retry; or labour exceeds the target. Revise before adding automation.

candidate.audience: Hypothesis: workplace teams at Riga social enterprises. The supplied seminar invitation identifies a relevant audience, not recurring demand. Start with two managers; team size, language and training needs remain unknown.
candidate.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: managers controlling training budgets would pay €15 per team monthly. The pilot would be free; no payment integration or sales claims. Ask who authorises purchases and whether €15 would replace or supplement current spending.
candidate.valueProposition: Proposed supplementary practice: discuss an illustrated hazard, submit one team answer, then compare it with a qualified reviewer-approved explanation. Not emergency advice, certification or a replacement for mandatory training.
candidate.firstTest: Within 14 days, founder would recruit two managers and secure qualified review of three scenarios. Cap total pilot cash at €39 and founder time at eight hours. Stop if review cannot fit. Compare with current checklists and the announced seminar; pass only if both request another round and identify a concrete added benefit.
candidate.mvp: Plan only; nothing has been contacted, built or tested. Use three reviewed illustrated scenarios, a private spreadsheet, team answer form and manual email delivery over three days. Reveal explanations after submission. Founder records flags and repeat requests. No accounts, leaderboard, AI-generated advice, billing or custom app. Separately rehearse the scheduled loop using dummy teams; do not promise an ongoing daily library from three scenarios.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain manager opt-in and team participation permission; collect team alias, one manager email and team-level choices only. No employee names, workplace photos or incident details. Founder alone accesses contacts; checker sees pseudonymous records; reviewer sees content only. Disable public sharing, verify vendor permissions and terms, store secrets separately, delete pilot responses and contacts after 30 days unless renewed consent.

architecture.tool: Existing email, form and private spreadsheet
architecture.why: Proposed baseline avoids a custom app. Verify available account permissions, costs and answer-reveal behaviour before selection. Compare its operator effort with a scheduler, not just feature counts.

architecture.tool: Versioned scenario files and restricted approval sheet
architecture.why: Store scenario ID, image version, answer key, explanation, reviewer approval and review date. Freeze approved bundles; any edit invalidates approval. No automatic content generation.

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions
architecture.why: Supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows. Propose a daily UTC job creating a delivery queue, not sending directly. Compare with manual preparation; automate only if a dummy rehearsal reduce

architecture.tool: Read-only validation script plus non-author human checker
architecture.why: Validate approval status, bundle version, answer mapping and explanation checksum before release. Independently reviewed safety accuracy remains a human responsibility; matching alone cannot establish

architecture.tool: Restricted spreadsheet with one human sender
architecture.why: Use team ID + local date + scenario version as a unique key. Track queued, checked, sending, sent, uncertain and failed. Record answer once per key; edits replace rather than append. Avoid concurrent

loop.trigger: At an agreed local time each pilot day, founder opens the queue; optional scheduled preparation uses a fixed UTC time with a documented local-time conversion. Manual fallback checks the queue if scheduling is late.
loop.make: Select an approved scenario not previously sent to that team. Create a dated bundle and unique delivery key. If no unseen approved content remains, stop and request review rather than silently repeat. Store the proposed challenge and reveal link.
loop.check: Separate checker compares image, answer options and explanation against the frozen approved bundle; script checks version, approval and duplicate key. Any mismatch blocks delivery. Qualified reviewer handles safety questions, not the script.
loop.deliver: Founder marks sending, sends one challenge, then records sent. After team submission, release only its checked explanation. Retry confirmed transient failures at most twice, 15 minutes apart. An uncertain send gets no automatic retry: inspect sent records and confirm status first.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing runs, bounces, duplicates, deletion and flags. Pause disputed content for all teams, notify affected managers and seek qualified reapproval. Never improvise safety corrections. If reviewer unavailable, withdraw the scenario; log resolution before resuming.

weeks.goal: Establish a safe, bounded pilot before building.
tasks: Founder would recruit two consenting managers and document existing training, purchasing authority and preferred cadence.
Obtain a qualified reviewer commitment and quote; agree an approval checklist covering ambiguity, local applicability and safe explanations.
Draft three original illustrations; stop if €39 cash or eight founder hours cannot cover the initial pilot.
Check form permissions and compare manual delivery with scheduled queue preparation.

weeks.goal: Run the initial human-led comparison only after approval.
tasks: Freeze three approved bundles and have a separate person verify presentation against the approved answers.
Send one scenario daily for three days; collect team choices before revealing explanations.
Ask each manager to compare usefulness with their current checklist and seminar expectations; seminar price and effectiveness remain unknown.
Record added benefit, ambiguity, delivery time and requests for another round; no claim of safety improvement.

weeks.goal: Rehearse operational failures before any automation decision.
tasks: With dummy teams, inject a wrong answer mapping, expired approval, duplicate trigger, missed schedule, failed send and uncertain send.
Verify blocked release, bounded retries, ledger recovery and founder escalation.
Compare manual preparation with an optional GitHub Actions queue prototype; retain manual delivery unless automation clearly saves time.
If both managers request more, seek separately approved content within the remaining budget; otherwise test recovery only.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue, simplify or stop.
tasks: Ask managers to choose daily, weekly or no further practice and explain what it adds.
Present the hypothetical €15 monthly offer; record budget authority and objections without treating stated interest as payment.
Calculate review, acquisition and support minutes; compare weekly practice with the daily proposal.
Delete pilot data on schedule, document unresolved risks and make a go/no-go decision before expanding content or hosting.

economics.hypothesis: €15 per team monthly might support reusable, reviewed practice, but daily new content may be uneconomic. Proposed volume is 10 teams, not a forecast. A weekly cadence is the lower-content-cost alternative.
economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions, not quotes: €20/hour labour, €5 monthly shared tools, €40 monthly shared content review, and 10 teams. Pilot cash ceiling €39 across all tests. Cloudflare's supplied $5 minimum is USD and excluded from this manual baseline.

Daily content could exceed the assumed review budget. No realised revenue or margin exists.

Acquisition effort: assuming one hour per team would cost €20 before any renewal.
Payment fees, VAT, refund costs and actual support burden; no checkout selected.

tests.hypothesis: Three reviewed scenarios add enough value for both managers to request more.
tests.test: Founder runs the consented three-day comparison within 14 days, €39 cash and eight founder hours; ask about existing training before showing scenarios.
tests.pass: Qualified review clears all three; both managers complete the comparison, request another round and name an added benefit.
tests.fail: Review exceeds bounds, any unsafe ambiguity remains, either manager declines more, or no concrete benefit over current practice emerges.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed loop prevents unchecked or duplicate delivery and recovers safely.
tests.test: Human runs six dummy failure cases: wrong key, revoked approval, duplicate trigger, missing run, transient failure and uncertain send. Use existing tools only.
tests.pass: All unsafe bundles blocked; zero duplicate deliveries; at most two confirmed-failure retries; uncertain sends paused; founder resolves every case in the ledger.
tests.fail: Any unchecked release, duplicate, unbounded retry or unresolved ownership. Keep delivery manual and revise.

tests.hypothesis: A recurring offer merits a larger purchasing test.
tests.test: In week four, founder presents daily and weekly options at a hypothetical €15 monthly and asks both managers to identify budget owner and next purchasing step.
tests.pass: Both identify an authorised payer and agree to a specific follow-up purchasing discussion; treat this only as a signal.
tests.fail: Neither option adds recurring value, purchasing authority is absent, or either manager rejects the proposed price without a viable alternative.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

hypotheses: Managers would pay €15 monthly for supplementary practice rather than rely on current training.
Daily scenarios provide enough additional value to offset interruption and content-review effort; weekly practice may be stronger.
Ten teams could share €40 monthly review and €5 tools; neither cost nor volume is validated.

Kill test: within 14 days, propose recruiting two managers, securing qualified review of three scenarios, and manually comparing them with each manager’s current approach. Cap cash at €39 and founder effort at eight hours, counting recruitment, delivery and follow-up. Stop before delivery if review
unknowns: Seminar price, content and effectiveness; existing checklist availability and adequacy.
A permission-based route to managers, response rate, acquisition minutes and purchasing authority. The invitation supplies no customer list or organiser endorsement.

Longer-term repeat use, payment and renewal. Three scenarios and requests for more cannot establish these.

plan.valueProposition: Proposed supplementary practice: discuss an illustrated hazard, submit one team answer, then compare it with a qualified reviewer-approved explanation. Not emergency advice, certification or a replacement for mandatory training.
plan.firstTest: Within 14 days, founder would recruit two managers and secure qualified review of three scenarios. Cap total pilot cash at €39 and founder time at eight hours. Stop if review cannot fit. Compare with current checklists and the announced seminar; pass only if both request another round and identify a concrete added benefit.
plan.mvp: Plan only; nothing has been contacted, built or tested. Use three reviewed illustrated scenarios, a private spreadsheet, team answer form and manual email delivery over three days. Reveal explanations after submission. Founder records flags and repeat requests. No accounts, leaderboard, AI-generated advice, billing or custom app. Separately rehearse the scheduled loop using dummy teams; do not promise an ongoing daily library from three scenarios.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain manager opt-in and team participation permission; collect team alias, one manager email and team-level choices only. No employee names, workplace photos or incident details. Founder alone accesses contacts; checker sees pseudonymous records; reviewer sees content only. Disable public sharing, verify vendor permissions and terms, store secrets separately, delete pilot responses and contacts after 30 days unless renewed consent.

loop.trigger: At an agreed local time each pilot day, founder opens the queue; optional scheduled preparation uses a fixed UTC time with a documented local-time conversion. Manual fallback checks the queue if scheduling is late.
loop.make: Select an approved scenario not previously sent to that team. Create a dated bundle and unique delivery key. If no unseen approved content remains, stop and request review rather than silently repeat. Store the proposed challenge and reveal link.
loop.check: Separate checker compares image, answer options and explanation against the frozen approved bundle; script checks version, approval and duplicate key. Any mismatch blocks delivery. Qualified reviewer handles safety questions, not the script.
loop.deliver: Founder marks sending, sends one challenge, then records sent. After team submission, release only its checked explanation. Retry confirmed transient failures at most twice, 15 minutes apart. An uncertain send gets no automatic retry: inspect sent records and confirm status first.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing runs, bounces, duplicates, deletion and flags. Pause disputed content for all teams, notify affected managers and seek qualified reapproval. Never improvise safety corrections. If reviewer unavailable, withdraw the scenario; log resolution before resuming.

Acquisition effort: assuming one hour per team would cost €20 before any renewal.

tests.hypothesis: Three reviewed scenarios add enough value for both managers to request more.
tests.test: Founder runs the consented three-day comparison within 14 days, €39 cash and eight founder hours; ask about existing training before showing scenarios.
tests.pass: Qualified review clears all three; both managers complete the comparison, request another round and name an added benefit.
tests.fail: Review exceeds bounds, any unsafe ambiguity remains, either manager declines more, or no concrete benefit over current practice emerges.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed loop prevents unchecked or duplicate delivery and recovers safely.
tests.test: Human runs six dummy failure cases: wrong key, revoked approval, duplicate trigger, missing run, transient failure and uncertain send. Use existing tools only.
tests.pass: All unsafe bundles blocked; zero duplicate deliveries; at most two confirmed-failure retries; uncertain sends paused; founder resolves every case in the ledger.
tests.fail: Any unchecked release, duplicate, unbounded retry or unresolved ownership. Keep delivery manual and revise.

tests.hypothesis: A recurring offer merits a larger purchasing test.
tests.test: In week four, founder presents daily and weekly options at a hypothetical €15 monthly and asks both managers to identify budget owner and next purchasing step.
tests.pass: Both identify an authorised payer and agree to a specific follow-up purchasing discussion; treat this only as a signal.
tests.fail: Neither option adds recurring value, purchasing authority is absent, or either manager rejects the proposed price without a viable alternative.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). learning.title: Allocate payment costs before testing the fee
learning.text: For this proposed €5 transaction, the supplied standard EEA card rate implies €0.325 in processing costs. That is 32.5% of the proposed €1 service fee if the organiser absorbs it. Define the cost bearer and measure remaining contribution during a human-run pilot; supplier pricing alone cannot establish willingness to pay or profitability.

sparring.question: What measured incremental recovery or labour saving, relative to direct florist surplus sales, should justify the €1 fee before extending beyond a manual pilot?
sparring.answer: The unresolved question is whether you create incremental florist value rather than move direct sales into a fee-bearing channel. None of the supplied receipts establishes that value. Before expanding, require incremental recovery plus labour savings, net of added handling and refund costs, to exceed €1 per collected bouquet by a margin agreed with the florist beforehand. Calculate this across all comparable surplus offered—not only bouquets that sell. One discriminating next test: within one florist, randomly assign comparable surplus batches to direct sales or your manual offer, holding price, bouquet quality and collection window constant.

loop.trigger: Each trading day florist confirms surplus quantity, quality floor, price and pickup cutoff. Independent checker approves the dated batch; absent approval or stale stock means no offer. Reservation requests after cutoff are rejected.

tests.hypothesis: One florist and three nearby buyers accept the proposed exchange.
tests.test: Human-run private pilot: obtain fee agreement, offer three €5 bouquets, and separately cancel an organiser-funded order before the agreed cutoff.
tests.pass: Florist accepts €1; all three buyers voluntarily pay and collect qualifying bouquets on time; organiser refund is confirmed within the agreed deadline; costs and minutes are logged.
tests.fail: Any fee refusal, missing purchase/collection, quality failure or unresolved refund fails this gate; do not interpret a pass as broad demand.

tests.hypothesis: Coordination adds value over direct florist reservations.
tests.test: Human-run comparison of two matched batches of up to three bouquets, logging stock, collections, florist minutes and organiser minutes.
tests.pass: Proposed threshold: equal or more collections, at least two florist minutes saved per collection, and organiser handling at most three minutes per collection.
tests.fail: No saved florist time, fewer collections or organiser handling above threshold; matched stock unavailable makes result inconclusive.

tests.hypothesis: A separate checker and idempotent workflow prevent unsafe completion.
tests.test: Human-supervised sandbox injects duplicate events, two last-unit requests, late payment, stock mismatch, notice error and refund failure.
tests.pass: No oversell, duplicate refund or fee; blocked mismatches; refund failure pauses sales and alerts owner within five minutes; all cases reconcile.
tests.fail: Any unsafe state, unowned exception or unresolved duplicate blocks live automation.

risks: Supplied city news and EU context do not establish local flower surplus or willingness to pay.
Three neighbours are a convenience sample; personal relationships may bias purchases.
Quality variation, no-shows and cannibalisation may erase florist value.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

loop.trigger: Proposed daily checks at 12:00 and 17:00 Europe/Riga, plus incoming player reports during a stated 12:00–19:00 service window. Outside that window show unknown after expiry; do not imply continuous monitoring.
loop.make: Founder logs court ID, observation time, receipt time, condition, evidence and report ID. Merge matching court/condition reports within 15 minutes while preserving evidence. Draft one version per court; reports are untrusted observations, never instructions.
loop.check: A separate checker confirms timestamps, rule provenance and evidence independently of the author. Reject future times and observations over two hours old. loop.deliver: Publish only approved versions to one read-only view with checked time and expiry. Use court ID plus observation time plus version as the publication key. loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns disputes, failed retries and missed checks. If the checker is unavailable, leave the draft unpublished and expire the prior observation. Mark uncertain fields unknown, notify affected participants of corrections and seek operator clarification for access disputes.

loop.trigger: Propose daily retrieval at 15:00 Europe/Riga, plus a final source recheck before the agreed 17:00 email cutoff. Founder monitors the run log. Retry fetch failures after 5 and 15 minutes, then switch to manual retrieval; never silently reuse yesterday's access claims.
loop.make: Drafter selects relevant official notices and records URL, content hash, retrieval time and stated effective interval. Produce a dated template with verified facts and unknowns. Treat all source text as untrusted data, never executable instructions. No source detail means no access recommendation.
loop.check: Separate human compares each claim with original text, checks freshness and conflicting notices, and records approve/reject with timestamp and version. Recheck sources immediately before release. Ambiguity, stale evidence or unavailable checker blocks access claims; uncertainty stays visible.
loop.deliver: Send only approved versions to opted-in recipients. Use firm+shift-date+brief-version as the delivery key; lock and record pending/sent status. Retry confirmed failures at most twice. For ambiguous send status, inspect sent mail before retrying. Corrections use a new version linked to the superseded briefing.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns failures, conflicts, bounces and corrections. By cutoff, send a clearly labeled verification-unavailable notice with source links, not an all-clear. Withdraw unsafe claims promptly and request acknowledgment of corrections. Weekly feedback updates the checklist; unresolved safety issues pause the pilot.

weeks.goal: Test usefulness before building automation.
tasks: Check source permissions, prepare consent text and recruit three dispatchers through appropriate public business contacts; stop after the six-hour cap if recruitment or three relevant shifts are unavailable.
Agree delivery cutoff, information language and a separate checker. Run the proposed three-shift comparison against original notices and current workflows.
Record use, planning benefit, reading minutes, checking minutes and unknowns. Continue only if the predefined usefulness threshold passes.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse a safe, repeatable manual loop.
tasks: Create the private register, briefing template, approval checklist, consent log and recipient/version delivery ledger.
Run controlled drills for outdated notices, conflicting times, absent checker, failed fetch, duplicate send and correction. These are simulations, not customer results.
Interview the likely payer about authority and a nonbinding €15 offer; record objections without treating stated interest as payment.

weeks.goal: Add minimal automation only if the manual gate passes.
tasks: Propose a small scheduled fetch and content-hash comparison using Actions; keep human drafting and independent release approval.
Add bounded retries, run logging, a delivery-key lock and a manual fallback checklist. Keep recipient data out of the code repository.
Compare measured manual effort with automation effort. Retain the spreadsheet/email workflow if automation adds fragility or saves little time.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue a limited service.
tasks: Repeat the briefing comparison on relevant shifts; log checking time, exceptions, delivery failures and concrete dispatcher feedback.
Review €15 price responses, shared versus per-firm labor, acquisition effort, fees and refund policy before proposing any paid continuation.
Continue only with useful repeat use and plausible costs; otherwise stop or narrow scope. Document deletion and unsubscribe handling; do not broaden corridor coverage yet.

economics.hypothesis: €15/month may work only if verification is shared across enough firms. All customer counts, prices, conversion and revenue are hypotheses. Free-pilot usage does not establish willingness to pay.
economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative monthly assumptions: 22 briefings, 15 shared human minutes each at €15/hour = €82.50 labor; €10 total hosting/email allowance, not a supplier quote. Checker time must fit within those minutes. Payment fees, taxes, refunds and acquisition remain unpriced. Cloudflare's supplied $5 minimum requires exchange-rate/tax checks.
economics.unitEconomics: At a hypothetical 10 firms: €150 gross revenue minus €82.50 shared labor and €10 tools leaves €57.50 before fees, taxes, refunds, acquisition and firm-specific support. At three firms, €45 minus €92.50 is -€47.50. Seven firms cover these illustrative shared costs only; this is not a demand forecast.
unknowns: Total drafter and separate-checker minutes per briefing, including exceptions.
Firm-specific support, acquisition hours, payment fees and refund exposure.
Willingness to pay and retention once these temporary works end.
Whether adequate verification is possible within the assumed labor budget.

tests.hypothesis: A checked briefing adds value beyond direct notices and current workflows.
tests.test: Human-run free pilot: three consenting dispatchers, three relevant shifts; alternate briefing-first and source-first review where feasible. Ask for a brief usage log and concrete planning benefit; collect no delivery addresses.
tests.pass: At least two use the briefing on all three shifts and each identifies a concrete incremental planning benefit. Record reading time rather than assuming savings.
tests.fail: Fewer than two meet both criteria, sources suffice, or three relevant shifts cannot be observed within the cap. Do not proceed to automation.

tests.hypothesis: The release process blocks unsafe claims and duplicate delivery.
tests.test: Human-run tabletop with six cases: stale notice, conflicting restriction, absent checker, fetch failure, ambiguous send and corrected source. Use drafts and a mock recipient ledger, not live access advice.
tests.pass: All six produce the specified hold, fallback or correction; zero unsupported access claims and zero duplicate mock sends.
tests.fail: Any unsupported claim is approved, uncertainty disappears, or an ambiguous send is blindly retried. Repair and repeat before release.

tests.hypothesis: Shared verification and payer interest justify investigating €15/month.
tests.test: Time five manual briefings, including both humans and exceptions. Ask three authorized buyers whether they would request a clearly labeled, nonbinding €15/month continuation offer.
tests.pass: Median total shared labor is at most 15 minutes per briefing and at least two buyers request an offer. This supports further testing, not revenue validation.
tests.fail: Labor exceeds the threshold or fewer than two request an offer. Reprice, narrow scope or stop; do not infer paid conversion.

risks: Night work does not establish a closure, permitted delivery access or a safe detour; the supplied excerpt lacks those details.
A fresh retrieval can still contain stale operational information. Briefings must not replace signs or official traffic directions.
Independent checking creates real labor and availability constraints; this MVP is deliberately not autonomous.
Temporary corridor coverage may end before acquisition costs are recovered.
Direct notices or existing dispatch tools may be sufficient; supplier capabilities and costs do not establish demand.
unknowns: Which reachable firms repeatedly cross the corridor during affected evenings?
Do authoritative notices provide sufficiently precise, current restrictions?
Who can independently check each briefing before the agreed cutoff?
Are collection, excerpt storage and email delivery permitted under the selected services and source terms?
What happens to repeat use and purchasing interest after roadwork ends?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

Recheck sources immediately before release. Ambiguity, stale evidence or unavailable checker blocks access claims; uncertainty stays visible.
loop.deliver: Send only approved versions to opted-in recipients. Use firm+shift-date+brief-version as the delivery key; lock and record pending/sent status. Retry confirmed failures at most twice. For ambiguous send status, inspect sent mail before retrying. Corrections use a new version linked to the superseded briefing.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns failures, conflicts, bounces and corrections. By cutoff, send a clearly labeled verification-unavailable notice with source links, not an all-clear. Withdraw unsafe claims promptly and request acknowledgment of corrections. Weekly feedback updates the checklist; unresolved safety issues pause the pilot.

weeks.goal: Test usefulness before building automation.
tasks: Check source permissions, prepare consent text and recruit three dispatchers through appropriate public business contacts; stop after the six-hour cap if recruitment or three relevant shifts are unavailable.
Agree delivery cutoff, information language and a separate checker. Run the proposed three-shift comparison against original notices and current workflows.
Record use, planning benefit, reading minutes, checking minutes and unknowns. Continue only if the predefined usefulness threshold passes.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse a safe, repeatable manual loop.
tasks: Create the private register, briefing template, approval checklist, consent log and recipient/version delivery ledger.
Run controlled drills for outdated notices, conflicting times, absent checker, failed fetch, duplicate send and correction. These are simulations, not customer results.
Interview the likely payer about authority and a nonbinding €15 offer; record objections without treating stated interest as payment.

weeks.goal: Add minimal automation only if the manual gate passes.
tasks: Propose a small scheduled fetch and content-hash comparison using Actions; keep human drafting and independent release approval.
Add bounded retries, run logging, a delivery-key lock and a manual fallback checklist. Keep recipient data out of the code repository.
Compare measured manual effort with automation effort. Retain the spreadsheet/email workflow if automation adds fragility or saves little time.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue a limited service.
tasks: Repeat the briefing comparison on relevant shifts; log checking time, exceptions, delivery failures and concrete dispatcher feedback.
Review €15 price responses, shared versus per-firm labor, acquisition effort, fees and refund policy before proposing any paid continuation.
Continue only with useful repeat use and plausible costs; otherwise stop or narrow scope. Document deletion and unsubscribe handling; do not broaden corridor coverage yet.

economics.hypothesis: €15/month may work only if verification is shared across enough firms. All customer counts, prices, conversion and revenue are hypotheses. Free-pilot usage does not establish willingness to pay.
economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative monthly assumptions: 22 briefings, 15 shared human minutes each at €15/hour = €82.50 labor; €10 total hosting/email allowance, not a supplier quote. Checker time must fit within those minutes. Payment fees, taxes, refunds and acquisition remain unpriced. Cloudflare's supplied $5 minimum requires exchange-rate/tax checks.
economics.unitEconomics: At a hypothetical 10 firms: €150 gross revenue minus €82.50 shared labor and €10 tools leaves €57.50 before fees, taxes, refunds, acquisition and firm-specific support. At three firms, €45 minus €92.50 is -€47.50. Seven firms cover these illustrative shared costs only; this is not a demand forecast.
unknowns: Total drafter and separate-checker minutes per briefing, including exceptions.
Firm-specific support, acquisition hours, payment fees and refund exposure.
Willingness to pay and retention once these temporary works end.
Whether adequate verification is possible within the assumed labor budget.

tests.hypothesis: A checked briefing adds value beyond direct notices and current workflows.
tests.test: Human-run free pilot: three consenting dispatchers, three relevant shifts; alternate briefing-first and source-first review where feasible. Ask for a brief usage log and concrete planning benefit; collect no delivery addresses.
tests.pass: At least two use the briefing on all three shifts and each identifies a concrete incremental planning benefit. Record reading time rather than assuming savings.
tests.fail: Fewer than two meet both criteria, sources suffice, or three relevant shifts cannot be observed within the cap. Do not proceed to automation.

tests.hypothesis: The release process blocks unsafe claims and duplicate delivery.
tests.test: Human-run tabletop with six cases: stale notice, conflicting restriction, absent checker, fetch failure, ambiguous send and corrected source. Use drafts and a mock recipient ledger, not live access advice.
tests.pass: All six produce the specified hold, fallback or correction; zero unsupported access claims and zero duplicate mock sends.
tests.fail: Any unsupported claim is approved, uncertainty disappears, or an ambiguous send is blindly retried. Repair and repeat before release.

tests.hypothesis: Shared verification and payer interest justify investigating €15/month.
tests.test: Time five manual briefings, including both humans and exceptions. Ask three authorized buyers whether they would request a clearly labeled, nonbinding €15/month continuation offer.
tests.pass: Median total shared labor is at most 15 minutes per briefing and at least two buyers request an offer. This supports further testing, not revenue validation.
tests.fail: Labor exceeds the threshold or fewer than two request an offer. Reprice, narrow scope or stop; do not infer paid conversion.

risks: Night work does not establish a closure, permitted delivery access or a safe detour; the supplied excerpt lacks those details.
A fresh retrieval can still contain stale operational information. Briefings must not replace signs or official traffic directions.
Independent checking creates real labor and availability constraints; this MVP is deliberately not autonomous.
Temporary corridor coverage may end before acquisition costs are recovered.
Direct notices or existing dispatch tools may be sufficient; supplier capabilities and costs do not establish demand.
unknowns: Which reachable firms repeatedly cross the corridor during affected evenings?
Do authoritative notices provide sufficiently precise, current restrictions?
Who can independently check each briefing before the agreed cutoff?
Are collection, excerpt storage and email delivery permitted under the selected services and source terms?
What happens to repeat use and purchasing interest after roadwork ends?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

evidence.quote: By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC.

tasks: Define the seven-day €20 offer and preregister separate buyer, engagement and reliability thresholds.
Draft two low-risk quests; independently verify sources, public access and Latvian. Limit preparation and outreach to four hours and €0 cash.
Invite three HR budget owners and two newcomers voluntarily; explain data use before collecting consent.
Compare quests with municipal links and a curated checklist. Record nonresponses; insufficient recruitment is inconclusive, not validation.

weeks.goal: Specify and prepare the concierge workflow only if week-one evidence warrants it.
tasks: Prepare seven quests plus two fallbacks for one neighbourhood, with versioned sources, expiry and independent sign-off.

economics.hypothesis: A €20 seven-day cohort pack might cover shared content maintenance if quests can be safely reused. Model at most five participants and 35 deliveries per pack; these are proposed limits, not observed traffic. No revenue or willingness to pay has been established.
economics.costAssumptions: Propose €0 pilot cash using already available tools, subject to availability. Value labour at an assumed €15/hour. The supplied Stripe quote is 1.5% + €0.25 for standard EEA cards; payment processing is deferred. Acquisition, checking, translation, support, tax and refunds must also be allocated.
economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetical €20 payment less the quoted €0.55 card fee leaves €19.45 before other costs. At assumed €15/hour, 45 minutes of allocated labour leaves €8.20 before acquisition, tax, refunds and tools; about 78 minutes consumes the full €19.45. Report setup separately, but do not treat it as costless.
unknowns: Actual checking, review, onboarding, exception and acquisition minutes.
Safe reuse across cohorts and neighbourhoods; frequency of source changes.
HR budget authority, purchase frequency, tax treatment and refund obligations.
Availability and permission controls of existing tools; any future supplier costs.

tests.hypothesis: HR values checked quests over municipal links and a curated welcome checklist at €20.
tests.test: Human shows both alternatives to three confirmed HR budget owners, varying presentation order. Ask preference, reason and nonbinding willingness to buy the defined pack. Take no payment.
tests.pass: At least one budget owner prefers the quest pack and records willingness to buy at €20 with a specific reason.
tests.fail: Zero qualifying buyers fails this threshold. Fewer than three interviews is inconclusive and blocks expansion.

tests.hypothesis: Newcomers complete a quest and voluntarily seek another.
tests.test: Two consenting newcomers try the checked prototype. Offer a clear way to request another quest; send no reminder for 24 hours. Ask afterward how it compared with the checklist.
tests.pass: Both complete one quest and at least one independently requests another within 24 hours. Report comparative usefulness separately.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed. Separate access failures from lack of interest; failure may favour a one-off pack rather than disprove all value.

tests.hypothesis: The manual workflow blocks unsafe or duplicate releases within a viable labour budget.
tests.test: Human rehearses expired approval, edited content, failed access, withdrawn consent, duplicate trigger, confirmed send failure and ambiguous send. Time a simulated seven-day workflow, including allocated shared checking.
tests.pass: All seven cases are blocked or reconciled correctly, retries obey limits, no duplicate occurs, and projected recurring labour is at most 45 minutes per cohort. Report setup separately.
tests.fail: Any unchecked, withdrawn-consent or duplicate release; blind ambiguous retry; or recurring labour above the target requires revision before expansion.

risks: The dated winterisation receipt supports changing local conditions, not current availability, route safety or customer demand.
Human checking and language review may cost more than the proposed price supports.
HR purchase intent and newcomer engagement may diverge; neither validates the other.
Private wins can reveal identity or location. Keep reporting optional and exclude individual activity from HR reports.
Manual reservations require a single sender; concurrent senders could defeat duplicate prevention.
Feedback could favour engaging but unsafe tasks; approval and expiry gates must remain independent.
unknowns: No actual customer contact, tests, users, payments, deployment or implementation has occurred.
Reachable HR buyers, newcomer needs and neighbourhood preferences remain unverified.
Checker availability, Latvian competence and public access require confirmation.
Source freshness beyond supplied receipts is unknown; current checks remain proposed.
Incremental value over a simple welcome checklist and willingness to pay remain unmeasured.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative monthly assumptions: 10 teams, €5 shared tools, €40 shared review, €20/hour labour and 10 support minutes per team. Review cost is not a quote. Pilot cash across all tests stays at €39. Cloudflare's supplied $5 USD minimum is excluded from this manual baseline.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Workers official pricing
evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

plan.valueProposition: Proposed supplementary practice: discuss an illustrated hazard, submit one team answer, then compare it with a qualified reviewer-approved explanation. Not emergency advice, certification or a replacement for mandatory training.

loop.trigger: At an agreed local time each pilot day, founder opens the queue; optional scheduled preparation uses a fixed UTC time with a documented local-time conversion. Manual fallback checks the queue if scheduling is late.
loop.make: Select an approved scenario not previously sent to that team. Create a dated bundle and unique delivery key. If no unseen approved content remains, stop and request review rather than silently repeat. Store the proposed challenge and reveal link.
loop.check: Separate checker compares image, answer options and explanation against the frozen approved bundle; script checks version, approval and duplicate key. Any mismatch blocks delivery. Qualified reviewer handles safety questions, not the script.
loop.deliver: Founder marks sending, sends one challenge, then records sent. After team submission, release only its checked explanation. Retry confirmed transient failures at most twice, 15 minutes apart. An uncertain send gets no automatic retry: inspect sent records and confirm status first.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing runs, bounces, duplicates, deletion and flags. Pause disputed content for all teams, notify affected managers and seek qualified reapproval. Never improvise safety corrections. If reviewer unavailable, withdraw the scenario; log resolution before resuming.

Draft three original illustrations; stop if €39 cash or eight founder hours cannot cover the initial pilot.
Check form permissions and compare manual delivery with scheduled queue preparation.

weeks.goal: Run the initial human-led comparison only after approval.
tasks: Freeze three approved bundles and have a separate person verify presentation against the approved answers.

Record added benefit, ambiguity, delivery time and requests for another round; no claim of safety improvement.

weeks.goal: Rehearse operational failures before any automation decision.
tasks: With dummy teams, inject a wrong answer mapping, expired approval, duplicate trigger, missed schedule, failed send and uncertain send.
Verify blocked release, bounded retries, ledger recovery and founder escalation.
Compare manual preparation with an optional GitHub Actions queue prototype; retain manual delivery unless automation clearly saves time.
If both managers request more, seek separately approved content within the remaining budget; otherwise test recovery only.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue, simplify or stop.
tasks: Ask managers to choose daily, weekly or no further practice and explain what it adds.
Present the hypothetical €15 monthly offer; record budget authority and objections without treating stated interest as payment.
Calculate review, acquisition and support minutes; compare weekly practice with the daily proposal.
Delete pilot data on schedule, document unresolved risks and make a go/no-go decision before expanding content or hosting.

economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions, not quotes: €20/hour labour, €5 monthly shared tools, €40 monthly shared content review, and 10 teams. Pilot cash ceiling €39 across all tests. Cloudflare's supplied $5 minimum is USD and excluded from this manual baseline.

Retention, team size, content reuse rights and willingness to pay.

tests.hypothesis: Three reviewed scenarios add enough value for both managers to request more.
tests.test: Founder runs the consented three-day comparison within 14 days, €39 cash and eight founder hours; ask about existing training before showing scenarios.
tests.pass: Qualified review clears all three; both managers complete the comparison, request another round and name an added benefit.
tests.fail: Review exceeds bounds, any unsafe ambiguity remains, either manager declines more, or no concrete benefit over current practice emerges.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed loop prevents unchecked or duplicate delivery and recovers safely.
tests.test: Human runs six dummy failure cases: wrong key, revoked approval, duplicate trigger, missing run, transient failure and uncertain send. Use existing tools only.
tests.pass: All unsafe bundles blocked; zero duplicate deliveries; at most two confirmed-failure retries; uncertain sends paused; founder resolves every case in the ledger.
tests.fail: Any unchecked release, duplicate, unbounded retry or unresolved ownership. Keep delivery manual and revise.

tests.hypothesis: A recurring offer merits a larger purchasing test.
tests.test: In week four, founder presents daily and weekly options at a hypothetical €15 monthly and asks both managers to identify budget owner and next purchasing step.
tests.pass: Both identify an authorised payer and agree to a specific follow-up purchasing discussion; treat this only as a signal.
tests.fail: Neither option adds recurring value, purchasing authority is absent, or either manager rejects the proposed price without a viable alternative.

A bounded next step is to ask managers what the proposed recurring practice adds to their current training and which budget could fund it; treat stated interest as a hypothesis until stronger human-run validation.

handoff.scopedMvp: Plan only; nothing has been contacted, built or tested. Use three reviewed illustrated scenarios, a private spreadsheet, team answer form and manual email delivery over three days. Reveal explanations after submission. Founder records flags and repeat requests. No accounts, leaderboard, AI-generated advice, billing or custom app. Separately rehearse the scheduled loop using dummy teams; do not promise an ongoing daily library from three scenarios.
validationGates: A human recruits actual people outside the simulated class.
A human runs the stated falsifiable test and records consent, observations and payments accurately.
A human reviews demand, unit economics, privacy, safety, failure handling and scope before authorizing a future pilot.

The seminar invitation supports topic relevance only; its price, content and effectiveness are unknown.

handoff.permissionsStatus: No implementation tools, outreach, deployment, payments or secrets are granted.

lastDraft.audience: Hypothesis: staff teams at Riga social enterprises. The supplied seminar invitation supports investigating this audience and topic, not recurring demand. Begin with two consenting managers; team size, language and accessibility needs remain untested.
lastDraft.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: a manager with training-budget authority would pay €15 per team monthly. Offer a free, bounded pilot, then ask which budget would fund continued use. No billing integration or payment claims in this MVP.
lastDraft.valueProposition: Proposed supplementary practice: identify hazards in an illustration, submit one team answer and compare it with a qualified reviewer-approved explanation. Test whether this adds value beyond existing checklists and training. Not certification, emergency advice or a substitute for mandatory training.
lastDraft.firstTest: Within 14 days, a human founder would recruit two managers and obtain qualified review of three scenarios. Total pilot cash ceiling: €39; founder effort: eight hours. Deliver nothing without approval. Compare with current checklists and seminar expectations. Pass only if both request another round and describe a specific added benefit.
lastDraft.mvp: Plan only: three approved illustrated scenarios, a restricted spreadsheet, an answer form and manual email delivery across three days. Reveal checked explanations after submission. Keep a delivery ledger and flag route. Rehearse failures with dummy teams. No custom app, accounts, leaderboard, AI advice, billing or ongoing daily-content promise.
lastDraft.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain manager opt-in and voluntary team participation; collect team alias, manager email and team-level choices only. No employee names, photos or incident reports. Founder accesses contacts; checker sees aliases; reviewer sees content. Verify vendor terms, access controls and retention before use. Disable public response lists; delete pilot contacts and answers after 30 days unless renewed permission.

architecture.tool: Existing email, form and restricted spreadsheet
architecture.why: Propose manual delivery before building an app. Verify permissions, costs and answer-reveal settings. Compare operator minutes and errors with scheduled preparation; retain this baseline unless automa

architecture.tool: Versioned files plus restricted approval sheet
architecture.why: Store scenario ID, image, options, answer key, explanation, reviewer identity, approval date and review scope. Freeze each approved bundle; any edit revokes approval until reviewed again. Use original

architecture.tool: Non-author human checker; optional read-only validation script
architecture.why: Compare the rendered challenge and reveal against the frozen approved bundle. Check approval, version, answer mapping and duplicate status. A script may detect mismatches, but cannot establish fire-sa

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions
architecture.why: The supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not reliable delivery or demand. Propose preparing a queue only; keep human sending. Use dummy records first. Adopt only if preparation time fa

architecture.tool: Restricted spreadsheet with one designated sender
architecture.why: Use team ID + local date + scenario ID as a delivery key, recording version separately. Track queued, checked, sending, sent, uncertain and failed. Maintain a team/scenario history to prevent repeats.

loop.trigger: At the agreed local time on each of three pilot days, founder checks the queue. An optional scheduled preparation job uses documented UTC-to-local conversion. Founder checks for a missing run before the delivery window closes; no automatic catch-up burst.
loop.make: Choose an approved scenario not previously sent to that team. Create the dated delivery key and freeze the challenge/reveal bundle. If the library is exhausted or approval is missing, stop. Three scenarios support three pilot days, not an indefinite daily rotation.
loop.check: A separate non-author checker verifies image, options, key and explanation against the approved version, plus consent and duplicate status. Mark checked only after all pass. Mismatch, revoked approval or missing permission blocks release; qualified review resolves safety uncertainty.
loop.deliver: Single sender reserves the key as sending, emails the challenge, then records sent. After one team answer, manually release its checked explanation. Retry confirmed transient failures at most twice, 15 minutes apart. For uncertain sends, inspect sent records before any resend; never retry blindly.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing runs, failed sends, duplicates, privacy requests and flags. Pause disputed content across teams, notify affected managers and refer safety questions to the qualified reviewer. Withdraw content if review is unavailable. Log correction and reapproval before resuming; never improvise safety guidance.

weeks.goal: Establish permissions, reviewer feasibility and a safe content gate.
tasks: Seek two consenting managers; ask about current training, recent difficulties, purchasing authority and preferred cadence before presenting the concept.
Seek a qualified reviewer quote and agree a checklist for ambiguity, local applicability, answer completeness and supplementary-use limits.
Draft three original illustrated scenarios; secure approval before delivery. Stop if the €39 cash or eight-hour founder cap cannot cover the initial pilot.
Configure a private ledger and answer form only after checking access, vendor terms and reveal behaviour. Arrange a separate non-author checker.

weeks.goal: Run the gated three-day human-led comparison.
tasks: Freeze the three reviewed bundles; have the separate checker validate each rendered challenge and explanation.
Send one scenario per day to each consenting team; collect its answer before manually releasing the checked explanation.
Ask managers to compare with their actual checklist or training; discuss the announced seminar as an alternative without assuming its content, price or effectiveness.
Record handling minutes, ambiguity, completion and requests for more. Pass the exploratory gate only if both managers name added value and request another round.

weeks.goal: Rehearse failures and compare manual operation with optional scheduling.
tasks: Use dummy teams to inject a wrong answer mapping, revoked approval, duplicate trigger, missing run, transient failure and uncertain send.
Verify blocked releases, duplicate prevention, retry limits and founder reconciliation in the ledger.
Compare five manual queue preparations with five scheduled rehearsals. Keep manual delivery; adopt queue automation only if its time saving meets the stated test.
If managers request more, seek new approved content within remaining bounds. Otherwise conduct dummy rehearsals only; do not recycle scenarios as fresh content.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to stop, simplify to weekly practice or fund another test.
tasks: Ask each manager to choose daily, weekly or no continuation, explaining what it adds to existing practice.
Present the hypothetical €15 monthly offer; identify an authorised budget owner and a concrete purchasing follow-up. Stated interest is not payment.
Calculate review, acquisition, creation and support minutes. Compare the daily proposal with a lower-content weekly alternative.
Document pass/fail results and unresolved risks. Apply deletion deadlines and decline expansion until content safety and operational gates pass.

economics.hypothesis: €15 per team monthly might fund reusable reviewed practice; daily fresh content could make it uneconomic. Ten teams is a planning scenario, not a forecast. Weekly delivery is the lower-content alternative. No revenue or customer demand has been established.
economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative monthly assumptions: 10 teams, €5 shared tools, €40 shared review, €20/hour labour and 10 support minutes per team. Review cost is not a quote. Pilot cash across all tests stays at €39. Cloudflare's supplied $5 USD minimum is excluded from this manual baseline.
economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetically, 10 × €15 = €150 monthly receipts; less €5 tools, €40 review and €33.33 support leaves €71.67 before creation, acquisition, fees, tax and refunds. One acquisition hour per team adds €200 initial labour. These assumptions do not establish profit; daily review could exceed the budget.
unknowns: Qualified reviewer rate, availability, review scope and content reuse rights.
Actual creation and support minutes, acquisition effort and renewal rate.
Payment fees, taxes, refunds and willingness to pay; no payment provider selected.
Whether weekly practice retains value while reducing review workload.

tests.hypothesis: Three reviewed scenarios add value beyond current practice.
tests.test: Founder runs the two-manager, three-day comparison within 14 days, €39 cash and eight founder hours. Obtain qualified approval first; ask about existing training before demonstrating scenarios.
tests.pass: All three scenarios clear review; both managers complete the comparison, request another round and identify a concrete added benefit.
tests.fail: Review exceeds bounds, unresolved ambiguity remains, either manager declines more or cannot identify added value. No unreviewed delivery.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed controls block unchecked and duplicate deliveries.
tests.test: A human runs six dummy cases: wrong mapping, revoked approval, duplicate trigger, missing run, transient failure and uncertain send.
tests.pass: Every invalid bundle is blocked; zero duplicate deliveries; no more than two confirmed-failure retries; uncertain sends pause; founder records every resolution.
tests.fail: Any unchecked release, duplicate, blind resend, unlimited retry or unowned exception. Revise controls and repeat before live use.

tests.hypothesis: Scheduled queue preparation saves enough effort to justify complexity.
tests.test: Human times five manual and five GitHub Actions dummy queue preparations using equivalent inputs; includes setup and recovery time separately.
tests.pass: Scheduled median preparation time is at least 30% lower, all queues match approved inputs, no duplicates occur and estimated setup payback is within four weeks.
tests.fail: Any correctness failure or failure to meet time and payback targets. Retain the existing-tool manual baseline.
