Matching an explanation to a key checks consistency, not safety truth.
Requests for another round may reflect novelty or politeness rather than retention or payment.
Review and founder labour may overwhelm the hypothetical €15 price.
Manual ledger errors remain possible; single-sender reservation and reconciliation must be rehearsed.
Three scenarios cannot sustain ongoing daily delivery; stop when approved unseen content is exhausted.
unknowns: No customer contact, tests, users, payment, deployment or implementation has happened.
Reviewer qualifications, independent checker availability and approval validity remain unconfirmed.
The seminar invitation supports audience/topic relevance only; price, attendance and effectiveness are unknown.
Team language, accessibility needs, preferred cadence and purchasing authority remain untested.
Existing-tool permissions, supplier terms and actual costs require verification.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.

This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

ideaSnapshot.title: Spot the Fire Risk
ideaSnapshot.line: Teams tackle daily illustrated fire-safety scenarios and compare answers against expert-reviewed explanations.
ideaSnapshot.test: Under €40: recruit two managers; test three expert-reviewed scenarios against a checklist; pass if both request another round.
ideaSnapshot.loop: Approved scenarios rotate daily; separate checks match explanations to reviewed answers; deliver team challenges; founder handles flags, pauses disputed content.

candidate.audience: Hypothesis: ten consenting adult recreational players near Nīcgales iela 15. The city receipt identifies a candidate sports complex, not public access or demand. Limit discovery to one operator-confirmed court.
candidate.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: nearby sports shops sponsor a clearly labelled line for €10/month; players use updates free. Seek nonbinding interest only after player usefulness passes. No sponsor, conversion or revenue is established.
candidate.valueProposition: Proposed benefit: check access rules and a recent surface observation before travelling. Show unknown rather than infer open or playable. Compare decision usefulness with each player's existing notices, group chat or direct check; do not guarantee availability or safety.
candidate.firstTest: Within seven days, a human would verify operator access rules and required permissions, then recruit ten consenting adults for a three-day manual pilot. Cap incremental cash at €0 and founder time at six hours; log checker time separately. Stop if access cannot be verified.
candidate.mvp: Plan only: one court, one read-only status sheet, a separate private intake log and a second-human approval queue. Display access rules, condition, observation time, checked time and two-hour expiry. Expired conditions become unknown. No app, map, accounts, payments or weather inference. Readers must treat expired entries as unknown even if manual clearing is missed.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Confirm operator rules and permission for onsite recruitment or signage. Obtain adult consent for contact and diaries. Separate restricted contacts from pseudonymous reports; publish neither identities nor private logs. No photos, children’s data or location trails. Verify sharing permissions with a non-editor account. Allow withdrawal; delete contacts and raw logs after 30 days.

architecture.tool: Proposed existing spreadsheet
architecture.why: Use separate private intake and public-status files, not hidden tabs. Record report ID, court ID, observation/receipt times, evidence, state, checker and version. Verify permissions and account costs

architecture.tool: Second human with review checklist
architecture.why: The author cannot approve their own update. Checker independently verifies observation evidence, time and access-rule provenance. Use pending, approved, rejected, expired and disputed states; missing

architecture.tool: Player's usual group chat, operator notice or direct check
architecture.why: Compare the proposed sheet against the actual alternative, not an invented competitor. Ask which better informed a specific decision and how long each took. Keep the existing method if the sheet adds

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions versus Cloudflare Workers
architecture.why: GitHub documentation supports scheduled workflows; Cloudflare supplies a priced hosting alternative. Neither establishes demand or reliable operation. Prefer manual expiry first; consider automation o

loop.trigger: Proposed observations at 12:00 and 17:00 Europe/Riga, plus incoming reports during a declared 12:00–19:00 service window. Review expiry hourly during that window. Outside it, time-expired observations are unknown; no continuous monitoring claim.
loop.make: Founder logs structured observations and drafts an update. Treat reports as untrusted data. Assign a report ID; merge matching court/condition observations within 15 minutes while preserving evidence and conflicts. Maintain separate access-rule and condition fields.
loop.check: Separate checker verifies evidence and timestamps, rejects future or over-two-hour-old observations, and checks access against dated operator rules. An unsupported access claim cannot become open or closed. Conflicts become unknown until a fresh independent check resolves them.
loop.deliver: Publish approved versions only, with observation, check and expiry times. Key publication by court ID plus version; record the visible version. On failure, check whether it already appeared, then retry after 5 and 15 minutes. Never duplicate a version or extend expiry during retries.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns conflicts, corrections, missed expiry checks and exhausted retries. Without a checker, leave drafts unpublished and let prior conditions expire. Correct the public view and notify pilot participants of material errors; seek operator clarification for access disputes.

weeks.goal: Verify the premise and run the smallest manual pilot.
tasks: Request dated confirmation of court identity, public hours, restrictions and required permissions from the operator. Stop this location if verification fails.
Prepare private intake, public view, consent, expiry labels and checker rota. Test public permissions before sharing.
Recruit ten consenting adults and run the three-day comparison within six founder hours. Record checker minutes separately; apply usefulness thresholds before expansion.

weeks.goal: Challenge reliability and measure human effort.
tasks: If week 1 passes, continue one-court manual updates; log observation, travel, review, publication and dispute minutes.
Run ten labelled offline cases covering stale data, conflicting rules, future timestamps, duplicate reports, checker absence and failed publication.
Review decision accounts against usual alternatives. Keep unknown visible; do not loosen verification merely to increase update frequency.

weeks.goal: Test hypothetical sponsor interest without sales claims.
tasks: Only after usefulness passes, invite three nearby shops to review the same anonymous summary and labelled sponsor mock-up.
Ask about €10/month, required audience evidence and a concrete nonbinding follow-up. Record refusals and acquisition minutes.
Keep sponsorship separate from status approval. Collect no payment and add no tracking pixels.

weeks.goal: Make a stop, manual-continuation or automation decision.
tasks: Summarise only results actually obtained; list blocked tests as unrun. Compare repeat consultation with specific decision usefulness.
Calculate full founder and checker labour, travel, acquisition and hypothetical sponsor contribution. Do not equate follow-up requests with revenue.

Continue manually only if usefulness and reliability pass. Consider expiry automation only if projected labour savings repay setup within four weeks; otherwise defer. Delete personal data on schedule.

economics.hypothesis: Illustration: three sponsors at proposed €10/month would yield €30/month gross. Sponsor count, price acceptance, acquisition and renewal are untested. A useful free pilot would not establish a viable business.
economics.costAssumptions: Target €0 incremental pilot software cost using existing access, subject to permission and pricing checks. Illustrative combined founder/checker labour: 20 minutes/day at €10/hour = €100 per 30 days, before travel and acquisition. Cloudflare's supplied paid minimum is $5 USD/month; defer it.
economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetical €30 gross minus €100 labour = −€70/month before tools, taxes, fees and travel. Ten €10 sponsors cover only that labour assumption. No payments in MVP; verify processing fees, tax treatment and refund terms before offering a paid pilot.
unknowns: Actual combined labour and travel cost per approved update.
Sponsor capacity, acquisition time, renewal and evidence requirements.
Account costs, payment fees, taxes, refund obligations and currency conversion.

tests.hypothesis: Fresh, checked updates inform decisions beyond players' usual alternatives.
tests.test: Human verifies access, recruits ten consenting adults and collects three-day consultation diaries and specific decision accounts. Cap founder effort at six hours; log checker effort separately.
tests.pass: Access and permissions verified; ten recruited; at least five each consult twice within three days; at least three describe a specific travel decision informed relative to their usual method.
tests.fail: Any gate or threshold is missed, or the founder cap is exceeded. Separate recruitment failure from usefulness failure; do not label consultation as an avoided trip.

tests.hypothesis: The manual loop contains unsafe, stale and duplicate claims.
tests.test: Two humans run ten labelled offline cases spanning stale/future observations, conflicting access, duplicates, checker absence and publication failures, including an ambiguous successful first publication.
tests.pass: All unverified or expired conditions remain unpublished or unknown; each approved version appears at most once; every exception has an owner and recorded disposition.
tests.fail: Any unsupported claim appears as current, a retry duplicates publication, or an exception is unowned.

tests.hypothesis: Nearby shops consider the proposed sponsorship worth further evaluation.
tests.test: After usefulness passes, a human shows three shops the same anonymous pilot summary and sponsor mock-up at €10/month; request a concrete nonbinding follow-up.
tests.pass: At least two request a concrete follow-up at the stated price and identify required evidence. Record this as interest only.
tests.fail: Fewer than two request follow-up, or interest requires unsupported audience or outcome claims.

risks: School-site infrastructure may not permit the proposed public use.
Conditions may change before expiry; observations cannot certify safety.
Sparse reports and unavailable checkers may leave most conditions unknown.
Manual clearing may be missed; prominent expiry must override the displayed condition.
Verification labour may exceed hypothetical sponsorship income.
Repeat consultation may reflect curiosity rather than decision value.
unknowns: Exact eligible court, verified access rules and required operator permissions.
Frequency of wasted trips and adequacy of existing information sources.
Achievable observation accuracy, freshness and independent-checker availability.
Reachable player audience and sponsor willingness to pay.
This is an implementation plan only. No actual contact, tests, users, payments, deployment or implementation has occurred.

candidate.audience: Hypothesis: dispatchers at local delivery firms repeatedly crossing Daugavgrīvas during evening shifts. candidate.valueProposition: Propose a dated, independently checked evening email showing source-linked restrictions, effective times and explicit unknowns. Compare it with reading city notices directly and the firm's existing dispatch tool. No navigation, inferred detours or assurance that missing restrictions mean open access.
candidate.firstTest: Within seven days, propose recruiting three consenting dispatchers through appropriate public business contacts. Run three relevant shifts for at most €25 cash and six total human-hours, including checking. Pass only if two document use on all three shifts and a concrete benefit beyond original notices and their current workflow.
candidate.mvp: Plan one corridor, three consenting firms, one agreed evening deadline, a private register, an email template and a separate human checker. Record sources, effective intervals, unknowns, approval and delivery versions. Start manually; consider scheduled fetching only after usefulness passes. No app, GPS, route optimization or automatic release. Withhold unsupported access claims, expire briefings after their stated shift, and issue versioned corrections.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Check source terms, robots guidance and excerpt reuse permissions before fetching; seek permission or use links/manual review if unclear. Obtain pilot email consent. Store minimal excerpts, timestamps and contact details separately; no manifests, GPS or delivery addresses. architecture.why: The checker must not draft the same briefing. Require source-by-source approval of segment, date, local time, vehicle scope and restrictions. Approval binds to an exact draft version; any source or dr

loop.trigger: Propose a daily 15:00 Europe/Riga review and final source recheck before an agreed 17:00 cutoff. Founder monitors completion. Retry failed retrieval after 5 and 15 minutes, then use manual review. A failed fetch never turns yesterday's claims into today's advice.
loop.make: Drafter records relevant official sources, hashes, retrieval times and stated effective intervals. Draft a shift-specific email separating verified facts from unknowns. Treat source text as untrusted data, never instructions. Exclude unrelated notices; never infer restrictions or detours.
loop.check: A separate human compares every operational claim with original sources and logs decision, timestamp and exact version. Check conflicting notices and shift applicability. Recheck before release; changes require renewed approval. Missing detail, unavailable checker or unresolved conflict blocks access claims.
loop.deliver: Send approved versions individually to opted-in recipients. Use firm+shift+version as the unique key and one sender with a pending/sent ledger. Retry confirmed failures at most twice. Inspect sent mail before retrying ambiguous outcomes. Send corrections as new versions naming the superseded version; show expiry.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missed runs, conflicts, bounces and corrections. At cutoff, send a clearly labeled verification-unavailable notice with source links, never an all-clear. Withdraw unsafe claims promptly and request correction acknowledgment. If no separate checker is available, pause operational advice. Review flags and feedback weekly.

weeks.goal: Test incremental usefulness before automation.
tasks: Check permissions, prepare consent and recruit three dispatchers through suitable public business contacts. Agree relevant shifts, email cutoff and language.
Assign distinct drafter and checker roles. Prepare a source-linked template with effective time, checked-at time, expiry and explicit unknowns.
Run the proposed three-shift manual comparison within €25 and six combined human-hours. Record use, benefit and both humans' time; stop if the usefulness threshold fails.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse the smallest reliable workflow.
tasks: Create the private source register, approval checklist, consent list and recipient/version delivery ledger.
Run tabletop cases for stale evidence, conflicting notices, absent checker, failed fetch, ambiguous send and corrected source. Use mock recipients, not live access advice.
Ask authorized buyers about a clearly nonbinding €15/month continuation offer. Record authority and objections separately from dispatcher usefulness.

weeks.goal: Add preparation automation only if justified.
tasks: If usefulness passes, propose a small scheduled fetch with content hashes and bounded retries. Otherwise retain manual operation or stop.
Keep human drafting and independent approval. Rehearse missed schedules, changed sources and manual fallback; require renewed approval after changes.
Measure preparation time against the manual baseline. Retain automation only if it saves at least 30% of preparation time without weakening checks and has projected setup payback within four weeks.

weeks.goal: Make a continue, narrow or stop decision.
tasks: Repeat comparisons on relevant shifts, if available. Review usefulness, checking minutes, unknowns, exceptions and delivery failures.
Model shared versus firm-specific work, acquisition, fees, taxes and refunds. Treat buyer interest as provisional, not revenue.
Continue only with repeated incremental usefulness and plausible economics. Otherwise stop or narrow coverage. Document unsubscribe, deletion and handover procedures; do not expand corridors yet.

economics.hypothesis: €15/month could work only if checking is fast and shared across enough firms. Proposed customer counts, conversion and revenue are hypotheses. Temporary roadwork may end before acquisition and setup costs are recovered.
economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative month: 22 briefings at 15 combined drafter/checker minutes each, valued at €15/hour, cost €82.50. Allow €10 for tools/email, not a supplier quote. Cloudflare's supplied $5 USD paid minimum needs exchange-rate and tax checks. Acquisition, payment fees, refunds and firm-specific support remain unpriced.
economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetical 10 firms yield €150 gross/month less €82.50 shared labor and €10 tools = €57.50 before other costs. Three firms yield a €47.50 shortfall. Seven firms cover these assumed shared costs only. This is a sensitivity calculation, not evidence that seven firms will buy.
unknowns: Combined drafting, checking and exception minutes per briefing.
Firm-specific support and acquisition hours.
Payment fees, taxes, refund exposure and actual tool costs.
Paid retention after the corridor works end.

tests.hypothesis: Checked briefings add repeat value beyond direct notices and existing tools.
tests.test: Human-run free pilot with three consenting dispatchers over three relevant shifts. Compare briefing-first and source-first review where feasible; collect usage, reading time and concrete benefits without delivery addresses.
tests.pass: At least two document briefing use on all three shifts and each identifies a concrete incremental planning benefit. Stay within €25 and six combined human-hours.
tests.fail: Fewer than two qualify, existing sources suffice, or relevant shifts/recruitment cannot be obtained within the cap. Do not automate.

tests.hypothesis: The release process blocks unsupported claims and duplicate sends.
tests.test: Human-run tabletop: stale notice, conflicting times, absent checker, fetch failure, ambiguous delivery and source correction. Use mock messages and the proposed ledger.
tests.pass: All six cases produce the specified hold, fallback or correction, with zero unsupported approved claims and zero duplicate mock sends.
tests.fail: Any unsafe claim passes, uncertainty disappears, approval survives a changed draft or ambiguous delivery is blindly retried. Repair and repeat before release.

tests.hypothesis: Shared verification effort and buyer interest justify further pricing investigation.
tests.test: Time five manual briefings including both humans and exceptions. Ask three authorized buyers whether they request a nonbinding €15/month continuation offer.
tests.pass: Median combined labor is at most 15 minutes per briefing and at least two buyers request an offer. This warrants further testing, not a claim of paid conversion.
tests.fail: Labor exceeds the threshold or fewer than two request an offer. Reprice, narrow scope or stop.

risks: Nighttime resurfacing does not establish a closure, delivery permission or safe detour.
Fresh retrieval can contain stale operational information; briefings must not replace road signs or official directions.
Independent checking introduces labor and availability constraints. This plan is not autonomous.
Direct notices or an existing dispatch tool may already solve the problem.
Temporary corridor value may not support retention or acquisition costs.
unknowns: Which reachable firms repeatedly cross the corridor during affected evening hours?
Do authoritative sources specify sufficiently current segments, times and vehicle restrictions?
Who can independently check before the agreed cutoff?
Are collection, storage and email practices permitted under selected source and service terms?
Would an authorized buyer actually pay after a useful free pilot?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns conflicts, corrections, missed expiry checks and exhausted retries. Without a checker, leave drafts unpublished and let prior conditions expire. Correct the public view and notify pilot participants of material errors; seek operator clarification for access disputes.

weeks.goal: Verify the premise and run the smallest manual pilot.
tasks: Request dated confirmation of court identity, public hours, restrictions and required permissions from the operator. Stop this location if verification fails.
Prepare private intake, public view, consent, expiry labels and checker rota. Test public permissions before sharing.
Recruit ten consenting adults and run the three-day comparison within six founder hours. Record checker minutes separately; apply usefulness thresholds before expansion.

weeks.goal: Challenge reliability and measure human effort.
tasks: If week 1 passes, continue one-court manual updates; log observation, travel, review, publication and dispute minutes.
Run ten labelled offline cases covering stale data, conflicting rules, future timestamps, duplicate reports, checker absence and failed publication.
Review decision accounts against usual alternatives. Keep unknown visible; do not loosen verification merely to increase update frequency.

weeks.goal: Test hypothetical sponsor interest without sales claims.
tasks: Only after usefulness passes, invite three nearby shops to review the same anonymous summary and labelled sponsor mock-up.
Ask about €10/month, required audience evidence and a concrete nonbinding follow-up. Record refusals and acquisition minutes.
Keep sponsorship separate from status approval. Collect no payment and add no tracking pixels.

weeks.goal: Make a stop, manual-continuation or automation decision.
tasks: Summarise only results actually obtained; list blocked tests as unrun. Compare repeat consultation with specific decision usefulness.
Calculate full founder and checker labour, travel, acquisition and hypothetical sponsor contribution. Do not equate follow-up requests with revenue.

Continue manually only if usefulness and reliability pass. Consider expiry automation only if projected labour savings repay setup within four weeks; otherwise defer. Delete personal data on schedule.

economics.hypothesis: Illustration: three sponsors at proposed €10/month would yield €30/month gross. Sponsor count, price acceptance, acquisition and renewal are untested. A useful free pilot would not establish a viable business.
economics.costAssumptions: Target €0 incremental pilot software cost using existing access, subject to permission and pricing checks. Illustrative combined founder/checker labour: 20 minutes/day at €10/hour = €100 per 30 days, before travel and acquisition. Cloudflare's supplied paid minimum is $5 USD/month; defer it.
economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetical €30 gross minus €100 labour = −€70/month before tools, taxes, fees and travel. Ten €10 sponsors cover only that labour assumption. No payments in MVP; verify processing fees, tax treatment and refund terms before offering a paid pilot.
unknowns: Actual combined labour and travel cost per approved update.
Sponsor capacity, acquisition time, renewal and evidence requirements.
Account costs, payment fees, taxes, refund obligations and currency conversion.

tests.hypothesis: Fresh, checked updates inform decisions beyond players' usual alternatives.
tests.test: Human verifies access, recruits ten consenting adults and collects three-day consultation diaries and specific decision accounts. Cap founder effort at six hours; log checker effort separately.
tests.pass: Access and permissions verified; ten recruited; at least five each consult twice within three days; at least three describe a specific travel decision informed relative to their usual method.
tests.fail: Any gate or threshold is missed, or the founder cap is exceeded. Separate recruitment failure from usefulness failure; do not label consultation as an avoided trip.

tests.hypothesis: The manual loop contains unsafe, stale and duplicate claims.
tests.test: Two humans run ten labelled offline cases spanning stale/future observations, conflicting access, duplicates, checker absence and publication failures, including an ambiguous successful first publication.
tests.pass: All unverified or expired conditions remain unpublished or unknown; each approved version appears at most once; every exception has an owner and recorded disposition.
tests.fail: Any unsupported claim appears as current, a retry duplicates publication, or an exception is unowned.

tests.hypothesis: Nearby shops consider the proposed sponsorship worth further evaluation.
tests.test: After usefulness passes, a human shows three shops the same anonymous pilot summary and sponsor mock-up at €10/month; request a concrete nonbinding follow-up.
tests.pass: At least two request a concrete follow-up at the stated price and identify required evidence. Record this as interest only.
tests.fail: Fewer than two request follow-up, or interest requires unsupported audience or outcome claims.

risks: School-site infrastructure may not permit the proposed public use.
Conditions may change before expiry; observations cannot certify safety.
Sparse reports and unavailable checkers may leave most conditions unknown.
Manual clearing may be missed; prominent expiry must override the displayed condition.
Verification labour may exceed hypothetical sponsorship income.
Repeat consultation may reflect curiosity rather than decision value.
unknowns: Exact eligible court, verified access rules and required operator permissions.
Frequency of wasted trips and adequacy of existing information sources.
Achievable observation accuracy, freshness and independent-checker availability.
Reachable player audience and sponsor willingness to pay.
This is an implementation plan only. No actual contact, tests, users, payments, deployment or implementation has occurred.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.

loop.make: s30 would update draft matches using stated budget, party size and weekend preferences. Record source/version and timestamps; merge on listing key rather than append duplicates. Publish neither inferred availability nor unconfirmed group capacity.

weeks.goal: Test permission, willingness to pay and paid reservation interest before building.
tasks: s30 would approach five operators and ten SSE students; s03 would cap effort at eight hours and cash below €30.

tasks: Offer no more than three verified sessions; run the daily maker/checker loop and log all exceptions and minutes.

weeks.goal: Test return behaviour and decide whether to continue.
tasks: Invite the original opt-in cohort to a second weekend shortlist without discounts; measure repeat requests and paid reservations.
Reconcile proposed commission against support time, acquisition effort, cancellations and collection costs.

economics.hypothesis: Illustrative assumptions, not forecasts: €30 per participant booking and 8% commission imply €2.40 gross platform revenue per completed booking. Count each paid participant booking consistently; a group enquiry alone earns nothing.
economics.costAssumptions: Operator-owned checkout means operator processing costs, not platform costs, unless negotiated otherwise. Supplied Stripe pricing is 1.5% + €0.25 for standard EEA cards: €0.70 on hypothetical €30. Assume founder labour at €12/hour and 10 minutes per completed booking; hosting and acquisition need separate allocation.
economics.unitEconomics: At those assumptions, €2.40 commission minus €2 labour leaves €0.40 before acquisition, hosting, tax and collection. If the platform absorbed €0.70 processing, contribution would be -€0.30. A hypothetical €20 acquisition spend over three completions adds €6.67 each; three reservations do not establish viability.
unknowns: Actual session prices, average group size, attendance and refund rates.
Operator acceptance of commission, referral attribution and invoice collection.
Acquisition cost, repeat demand and human minutes per completed booking.
Payment-provider terms, taxes, currency conversion and any additional platform fees.

tests.hypothesis: Operators will authorise supply at 8%, and students will pay for the proposed offer.
tests.test: Human-run, seven-day outreach to five operators and ten students; offer only authorised sessions with explicit terms and operator checkout. No discounts or founder-funded reservations.
tests.pass: At least two operators agree in writing and three distinct students make operator-confirmed paid reservations; spend below €30 and effort at most eight hours.
tests.fail: Any threshold missed, or permission/payment evidence unavailable. Do not interpret interest or unpaid holds as paid reservations.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed control loop prevents stale listings and duplicate handoffs.
tests.test: s14 would run ten synthetic cases, including stale data, changed prices, sold-out capacity, repeated submissions, failed sends and ambiguous booking responses.
tests.pass: All unsafe cases suppressed; zero duplicate booking handoffs or sends; every unresolved case assigned to s03 with an audit trail.
tests.fail: Any unsafe publication, duplicate handoff, blind booking retry or unowned exception. Fix and rerun before a pilot.

tests.hypothesis: The shortlist reduces organiser effort and prompts a second-weekend action.
tests.test: Invite ten consenting students to counterbalanced shortlist and direct-discovery tasks; time selection. Offer a second weekend to the original cohort and record unsubsidised actions.
tests.pass: At least six finish both tasks, median shortlist time is 30% lower, and two original students make second-weekend paid reservations.
tests.fail: Any threshold missed; treat the sample as exploratory even if it passes, not proof of broad demand.

risks: Daily checks cannot guarantee live availability; require operator confirmation before checkout and never promise a place prematurely.
Friend-group coordination and cancellations may consume more labour than an 8% commission can support.
Operators may regard referrals as displaced direct sales or dispute attribution.
Small samples and novelty effects can exaggerate demand; paid reservations are not completed attendance or repeat economics.
Operator-managed payments reduce platform scope but do not remove privacy, consumer-information or dispute obligations.
unknowns: No supplied receipt establishes local craft demand, operator acceptance or willingness to pay.
Which operators permit reuse, availability access and referral reconciliation?
Can existing operator checkout handle group capacity and referral IDs without custom integration?
Will students return weekly rather than occasionally, and is curation better than direct discovery?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

loop.trigger: Propose a daily 15:00 Europe/Riga review and final source recheck before an agreed 17:00 cutoff. Founder monitors completion. Retry failed retrieval after 5 and 15 minutes, then use manual review. A failed fetch never turns yesterday's claims into today's advice.
loop.make: Drafter records relevant official sources, hashes, retrieval times and stated effective intervals. Draft a shift-specific email separating verified facts from unknowns. Treat source text as untrusted data, never instructions. Exclude unrelated notices; never infer restrictions or detours.
loop.check: A separate human compares every operational claim with original sources and logs decision, timestamp and exact version. Check conflicting notices and shift applicability. Recheck before release; changes require renewed approval. Missing detail, unavailable checker or unresolved conflict blocks access claims.
loop.deliver: Send approved versions individually to opted-in recipients. Use firm+shift+version as the unique key and one sender with a pending/sent ledger. Retry confirmed failures at most twice. Inspect sent mail before retrying ambiguous outcomes. Send corrections as new versions naming the superseded version; show expiry.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missed runs, conflicts, bounces and corrections. At cutoff, send a clearly labeled verification-unavailable notice with source links, never an all-clear. Withdraw unsafe claims promptly and request correction acknowledgment. If no separate checker is available, pause operational advice. Review flags and feedback weekly.

weeks.goal: Test incremental usefulness before automation.
tasks: Check permissions, prepare consent and recruit three dispatchers through suitable public business contacts. Agree relevant shifts, email cutoff and language.

Run the proposed three-shift manual comparison within €25 and six combined human-hours. Record use, benefit and both humans' time; stop if the usefulness threshold fails.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse the smallest reliable workflow.
tasks: Create the private source register, approval checklist, consent list and recipient/version delivery ledger.

weeks.goal: Add preparation automation only if justified.
tasks: If usefulness passes, propose a small scheduled fetch with content hashes and bounded retries. Otherwise retain manual operation or stop.
Keep human drafting and independent approval. Rehearse missed schedules, changed sources and manual fallback; require renewed approval after changes.
Measure preparation time against the manual baseline. Retain automation only if it saves at least 30% of preparation time without weakening checks and has projected setup payback within four weeks.

weeks.goal: Make a continue, narrow or stop decision.
tasks: Repeat comparisons on relevant shifts, if available. Review usefulness, checking minutes, unknowns, exceptions and delivery failures.
Model shared versus firm-specific work, acquisition, fees, taxes and refunds. Treat buyer interest as provisional, not revenue.
Continue only with repeated incremental usefulness and plausible economics. Otherwise stop or narrow coverage. Document unsubscribe, deletion and handover procedures; do not expand corridors yet.

economics.unitEconomics: Hypothetical 10 firms yield €150 gross/month less €82.50 shared labor and €10 tools = €57.50 before other costs. Three firms yield a €47.50 shortfall. Seven firms cover these assumed shared costs only. This is a sensitivity calculation, not evidence that seven firms will buy.

Payment fees, taxes, refund exposure and actual tool costs.
Paid retention after the corridor works end.

tests.hypothesis: At least five of ten invited students return without reminders.

tests.pass: At least five original invitees attend both weeks; all used stops have documented access approval; spend ≤€20 and effort ≤six hours.
tests.fail: Any gate missed, including cancellation or insufficient safe access. Record why rather than relaxing thresholds.

tests.hypothesis: Some local shops would conditionally buy the defined €20 weekly offer.
tests.test: After an attendance pass, a human presents the same offer to five shops, including labelled placement and consented aggregate reporting. Request a written conditional commitment; take no payment.
tests.pass: At least two shops explicitly accept €20 conditional on stated delivery terms; record acquisition time and remaining conditions.
tests.fail: Fewer than two commitments, or required outcomes cannot be delivered safely and privately. Commitments remain weaker than paid renewal.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed controls prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.
tests.test: Human-run tabletop replay: stale access, absent checker, duplicate trigger, failed preparation, uncertain send and withdrawal. Use synthetic records only.
tests.pass: Every unsafe case is blocked, no session is sent twice, retries stop at two, and s18 records each exception and resolution.
tests.fail: Any unapproved release, duplicate, exposed participant record or unowned exception; retain manual delivery and revise controls.

risks: A school-site announcement does not establish unrestricted access, opening hours or workout suitability.
Weather, injuries and changing equipment conditions require cancellation authority, not automated reassurance.
Friendship and novelty may explain return attendance; this small pilot cannot isolate roulette's effect.
Shared streaks can disclose routines or create pressure; keep participation optional and avoid individual rankings.
Human inspection and sponsor acquisition may overwhelm €20 weekly revenue.
Tool documentation and supplier prices establish neither successful operation nor customer demand.
unknowns: Who can grant access and what restrictions apply at each candidate stop?
Is competent independent exercise review available within the pilot limits?
Do participants prefer roulette to a plain invitation, and does it affect return behavior?
Which sponsor benefit is valuable without sharing participant identities?
Can weekly inspection and exception handling remain affordable without weakening checks?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

economics.unitEconomics: Target steady-state labor hypothesis: 60 minutes per sponsored week, costing €12 at the assumed rate. €20 revenue less €12 labor leaves €8 before software, acquisition, fees, tax, refunds and insurance. Whether any shop accepts €20 and what reporting it requires.
Payment method, fees, tax treatment and insurance needs before charging.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

loop.trigger: Proposed 09:00 Europe/Riga daily checklist for seven days. s10 reviews consent status, incidents and unresolved reservations. s37 confirms withdrawals before sending. A 09:30 missed-trigger check prompts manual recovery, not bulk catch-up.
loop.make: s37 drafts a tiny task, duration, reviewed phrase, source, access notes and fallback. Select an unseen eligible quest. Optional feedback adjusts tomorrow's ranking, never approval. loop.check: s21 independently checks current access, instructions and phrase accuracy. Proposed expiry: seasonal/event details within 24 hours; stable quests within seven days. Edits invalidate approval. Missing, expired or failed checks block release; substitute only an approved, unseen fallback.

tasks: Run synthetic failure drills before any proposed live delivery; repair failed gates before proceeding.

unknowns: Actual recurring checking, language review, onboarding and exception minutes.

Tool availability, payment fees, tax treatment and refund exposure.

tests.hypothesis: HR prefers checked quests over municipal links and a curated checklist at €20.

Feedback must never promote an engaging quest past a failed safety or freshness gate.

Reachable HR buyers, newcomer needs and neighbourhood preferences remain unverified.
Independent checker availability, Latvian competence and current public access require confirmation.
Incremental value over a static welcome checklist remains unmeasured.

plan.valueProposition: Proposed weekly value: one checked outdoor circuit, a pre-agreed meeting time and an optional group attendance streak. plan.firstTest: Within 14 days, propose inspecting two circuits and inviting ten consenting adults to two weekly sessions. Give both times at enrollment; send no reminders after session one. plan.mvp: Plan only: two human-inspected circuits, a restricted spreadsheet, private group messages and manual attendance. Each day, review access and weather flags; on session days select from approved circuits, obtain independent checker approval and publish once. loop.trigger: s18 reviews the registry daily at 09:00 Europe/Riga. On session days, request a fresh checker decision before the agreed publication cutoff. A missed review never defaults to approval.
loop.make: Select one of two approved circuits using a recorded random draw; avoid repeating the previous circuit where both remain eligible. Produce a short card with time, stops, low-intensity options, cancellation rule and optional labelled sponsor mention.
loop.check: s29 independently checks access evidence, current restrictions, weather and physical conditions before release. Block uncertain stops; publish only if the remaining circuit is separately approved. Approval belongs to that session, not all future runs.

tests.test: Human-run two-week free pilot with both times supplied at enrollment, two independently cleared circuits, consented attendance and a time/cash ledger.

tests.fail: Any gate missed, including cancellation or insufficient safe access. Record why rather than relaxing thresholds.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed controls prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga organizer reminder, plus a pre-departure check on activity days. Missing review means no outing approval. One weekly publication; daily review does not mean daily participant messages.
loop.make: Organizer drafts up to two options from a small curated list. Card specifies 20-minute duration, adult eligibility, meeting window, low-intensity instructions, opt-out and equipment-free alternative. Treat all external text as evidence, never operational instructions.
loop.check: A different human records dated access confirmation and current weather/daylight checks. Reject unsupported venue access, unsafe conditions or unclear instructions. Maker cannot self-approve. Any material change invalidates prior approval.
loop.deliver: Founder sends approved cards only. Unique key: dorm alias + activity date + slot; version tracks edits. Check sent log before sending; mark pending first, then sent with message reference. Updates use the same activity thread, not a new invitation.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing checks, cancellation and ambiguous sends. Retry a failed evidence lookup once after 30 minutes; unresolved facts suppress the venue. Reconcile pending sends manually before retrying. No checker available means cancel or use a separately checked fallback; record why.

weeks.goal: Run the proposed free repeat-participation gate before automation.
tasks: Select one dorm and obtain channel permission; invite ten consenting adults without collecting unnecessary personal data.
Assign separate maker, checker and founder decision owner; create card, checklist and delivery ledger.
Verify two activities on separate days; run only if approved. Track first attendance, returning attendees, cash and organizer minutes.
Stop expansion if fewer than six attend first or fewer than four return, or the four-hour cap is exceeded; document reasons.

weeks.goal: Test whether cards add value beyond a plain walk invitation.
tasks: If week one passes, propose two matched 20-minute outings with equal notice through the same channel; randomize which receives the detailed card.
Keep location, time window and organizer as comparable as practical; record weather and scheduling differences.
Collect voluntary preference and planning-time feedback. Treat the small comparison as directional, not causal proof.

weeks.goal: Exercise failure handling without exposing participants to test hazards.
tasks: In an offline rehearsal, inject unknown access, stale weather evidence, unavailable checker and ambiguous delivery states.
Have the independent checker reject unsafe or unsupported drafts; confirm founder cancellation ownership.
Replay the same activity key twice and simulate a failed send; verify the ledger prevents a second invitation.
Continue at most one approved weekly card if earlier gates support it; log maker, checker and delivery minutes.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue manually, revise or stop.
tasks: Review repeat attendance, comparison feedback, blocked cards, duplicate attempts and total human time.
Estimate recurring cost using recorded minutes; do not infer sponsor willingness from free attendance.
Continue manual delivery only if usefulness and safe review appear repeatable; otherwise simplify to walks or stop.
Document any future automation requirement without deploying it; delete or anonymize records on the stated schedule.

economics.hypothesis: Free participation may justify a small manual wellbeing activity, not yet a business. Proposed four-week incremental cash budget is €0 using already available tools; sponsor revenue is untested and excluded.
economics.costAssumptions: Week-one labor cap: four hours; proposed later cap: one hour weekly, seven hours total. At an illustrative €15/hour opportunity cost, total labor is €105. Assumes volunteer time, no travel purchases, equipment, paid software or payment fees.
economics.unitEconomics: Revenue per participant: €0. At four retained participants, illustrative four-week labor cost is €26.25 each (€105/4), with cash contribution €0 before labor. This is a scenario, not an observed result; acquisition and checking time must be measured.
unknowns: Actual organizer and checker minutes, including recruitment and cancellations.
Whether existing tools and suitable nearby locations permit a genuinely €0 incremental test.
Whether any organization would fund ongoing labor; no sponsor interest is established.

tests.hypothesis: Ten invited adults will show repeat participation without purchases.
tests.test: Human organizer invites ten consenting adults to two checked activities within seven days; count attendance by alias and log all organizer minutes.
tests.pass: At least six attend first and at least four of those return for second; incremental cash €0 and organizer time at most four hours.
tests.fail: Any threshold is missed, or checks cannot establish a suitable outing. Revise or stop rather than automate.

tests.hypothesis: Cards offer more useful planning support than a plain walk invitation.
tests.test: After the first gate, compare two matched outings through the same channel, randomizing card order. Ask attendees who saw both invitations which format helped and why; record preparation time.
tests.pass: At least six give feedback, at least four prefer the card for a concrete planning reason, and card preparation adds no more than 15 minutes.
tests.fail: Any threshold is missed; favor plain invitations or repeat a better-matched comparison rather than claim differentiation.

tests.hypothesis: Independent review and a delivery ledger block unsafe drafts and duplicate sends.
tests.test: Human-run offline rehearsal: unknown access, stale conditions, missing checker, failed send and duplicate activity key. No participant receives rehearsal messages.
tests.pass: All unsafe or unchecked cases are blocked; duplicate replay produces zero extra sends; ambiguous send is held for founder reconciliation.
tests.fail: Any unsafe draft is approved, duplicate is sent or exception lacks an owner; halt delivery and repair the checklist.

A human checker can share the maker's assumptions; require underlying evidence and explicit unknowns.
Weather, darkness, unequal physical abilities and cancellations may undermine inclusion; permit opting out without explanation.
Manual messaging cannot guarantee atomic delivery; ambiguous status requires reconciliation, not blind retries.
unknowns: Which dorm permits recruitment, and which language and schedule fit consenting adults?
Which locations have confirmed access and appropriate conditions at the intended times?
Can a genuinely separate checker be available within the time budget?
Do residents want weekly cards rather than an ordinary friend-organized walk?
No customer contact, users, payments, deployment, implementation or real-world results have occurred.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
